summary: For ages 7-9 (Lower KS2 / Grades 2-4), this procedural topic teaches children to use a dichotomous (branching yes/no) classification key to identify minibeasts, and crucially to understand WHY a fixed order of feature-based questions can identify a creature they have never seen before, as long as that creature is one the key includes. It aligns to UK DfE KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (explore and use classification keys to group, identify and name living things) and loosely supports US NGSS life-science practices of observing and comparing traits. Learners both FOLLOW a given key and BUILD their own, choosing good splitting questions. The core insight: a key works on creatures you do not recognise, provided they are in the key, because it asks about observable features, not names. (The classic question 'Does it have six legs?' is used to separate insects from spiders in a small minibeast set, not as a full definition of 'insect'.)
misconceptions: 'A key identifies by name/appearance' — it works by asking about observable features, which is why it handles unknown creatures.
'Questions can be in any order' — the order structures the narrowing; a good key splits systematically.
'Any question will do' — a useful question must cleanly divide the remaining set into two.
'If I don't recognise the creature I can't identify it' — the key's whole point is identifying the unfamiliar.
Choosing subjective questions ('is it scary?') that don't reliably split organisms.

activities.title: Identify a mystery minibeast by walking a key
steps: Use a small branching key (4-6 creatures) to identify a minibeast you cannot see all at once — you can only answer questions about it.
Trace the ONE mystery creature: 'Does it have legs?' → yes, so the legless candidates (e.g. worms, snails) drop out of a row of possibilities.
Continue the SAME creature: 'Six legs?' → no, eight; the insects fall away, leaving the arachnids. 'Two body parts?' → yes; the last card flips to reveal a spider.

Now, as a separate task, work through the key for at least four different minibeasts (e.g. ant, spider, woodlouse, snail): for EACH one, start at the top question and follow the branch that ITS own answers point to until you reach a name — different creatures take different branches.
For each identification, name which single answer along the way ruled out a wrong group (e.g. which answer ruled out 'insect').
activities.insight: A key identifies by asking about observable features in a set order; each answer narrows the remaining possibilities, so an ordered sequence of questions can pin down even a creature you have never met, as long as it is one of the creatures the key includes.

activities.title: Build your own key and test it
steps: Take a set of six minibeasts and build your own branching key, choosing the yes/no question at each fork.

Write questions that use an observable, unambiguous feature that cleanly splits the remaining group into two. For example, 'Does it have six legs?' separates insects from spiders in this set (yes: the six-legged insects / no: the eight-legged spiders, plus any other legged creatures without six legs, such as a woodlouse with 14 legs).
Test each question on two known creatures: do they give different answers? If a woodlouse and an ant give the same answer, that question won't split them — revise it.
Avoid subjective or vague questions ('Is it scary?', 'Is it pretty?', 'Is it big?') because different people answer them differently for the same creature.

Swap keys with a partner and use their key to identify creatures from their set without being told the names, fixing any fork where a creature gets stuck or mis-sorted. Then run a creature that is NOT in the set through a key: notice that it gets stuck or lands on a wrong name, because a key can only name creatures it includes. Extend the key by adding a new question and end point for it.
activities.insight: Building a key forces you to choose good splitting questions: each must have a clear yes/no answer and genuinely divide the remaining set, revealing the underlying logic of why a key is reliable.

activities.title: Reasoning practice: order and choice of questions
steps: Given two minibeasts, choose which of several questions best splits them apart, and explain why the others fail.
Put a set of jumbled key steps into a sensible order so the questions narrow systematically.
Explain in your own words why a fixed order of questions helps you identify a creature you have never seen (as long as it is in the key), rather than just guessing.
activities.insight: Choosing the best splitting question and ordering questions deliberately both depend on the same idea: good questions use clear, observable features and each one narrows the set.

checkQuestion: Here is a simple branching key and four minibeasts to identify (e.g. ant, spider, woodlouse, snail). Work through the key out loud for each creature and tell me what each one is. Then I'll give you a creature that ISN'T on the key — make up a yes/no question that would split the insects from the spiders, and show me where it would go.
checkAnswer: The child starts at the first question of the key and answers each yes/no in order, following the branch its answer points to, until they reach a name — correctly identifying at least four minibeasts. When asked to extend the key, they write a question with a clear yes/no answer that genuinely separates the groups (e.g. 'Does it have six legs?' → yes: insect / no: not) and place it at a sensible branch point.
